passage:
Few doctrines in the common law of torts have proved more resilient, or more troubling, than the rule that a landowner owes only a minimal duty of care to persons who enter her land without permission. Under the traditional formulation, still recited in many jurisdictions, the occupier must merely refrain from willfully injuring the trespasser; the elaborate apparatus of reasonable foreseeability that governs other negligence cases has no application. The rule is often defended on the ground that it protects the autonomy of the landowner and discourages wrongful entry. Yet in a series of decisions beginning in the late 1970s, the High Court of the fictitious jurisdiction of Alderney began to qualify the rule in ways that have not been fully appreciated.

The turning point was the 1981 decision in a case involving a child who had wandered onto an unfenced construction site and been injured by exposed machinery. Rather than disturb the traditional rule outright, the court carved out what it termed a "known-peril exception," under which an occupier who is aware that trespassers regularly frequent a particular portion of her land may be required to take reasonable steps to abate latent dangers there. The exception was initially confined to cases involving children, on the theory that minors cannot reliably appreciate the significance of a no-trespassing sign. In subsequent decisions, however, the court extended the doctrine to adult trespassers whose presence was, as a factual matter, anticipated by the occupier — hikers crossing a pasture to reach a beach, for instance, or commuters using an unmarked path across a rail yard.

Critics have argued that this expansion has hollowed out the traditional rule while leaving its language intact, producing a doctrine that is nominally strict but functionally indistinguishable from ordinary negligence. The charge has some force; the distinction between a peril that is "known" to the occupier and one that is merely foreseeable to a reasonable occupier is finer than the court's opinions have acknowledged, and in practice the two inquiries tend to collapse into each other. Yet the criticism overstates the case. The Alderney court has consistently declined to extend the exception to trespassers whose presence was not actually anticipated, and it has refused to require affirmative inspection of the premises for hidden dangers. The occupier is still entitled, in most cases, to assume that her land is hers to use as she wishes.

What the Alderney decisions illustrate, then, is not the abandonment of the traditional rule but its gradual domestication. The court has been unwilling to say, as courts in some neighboring jurisdictions have said, that the status of the entrant is simply one factor among many in an undifferentiated negligence calculus. Whether that reticence will survive the next generation of cases is, regrettably, uncertain.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Alderney High Court's known-peril exception has effectively abolished the traditional rule governing a landowner's duty to trespassers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although critics have charged that recent Alderney decisions have hollowed out the traditional rule on duty to trespassers, the court has in fact modified the rule only in limited ways while preserving its core.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The traditional common-law rule that a landowner owes trespassers only a duty to avoid willful injury is difficult to reconcile with ordinary principles of negligence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts should extend the known-peril exception developed in Alderney to cases involving adult trespassers whose presence is not actually anticipated by the occupier.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Alderney High Court's 1981 decision concerning a child injured on a construction site marked a decisive break with the traditional rule governing trespassers.

explanations.correct: The passage sets up the traditional rule, describes the Alderney court's qualifications, acknowledges the critics' charge that the rule has been gutted, and then responds that the criticism overstates the case — the court has modified but preserved the traditional rule. B integrates both strands.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's corrective: the author explicitly argues the court has not abandoned the traditional rule.
explanations.C: The passage does not argue that the traditional rule is irreconcilable with ordinary negligence; it describes how the Alderney court has navigated between the two.
explanations.D: The author reports that the court has declined to extend the exception to unanticipated trespassers, without endorsing further extension.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement — the 1981 case is an illustrative turning point, not the thesis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the critics described in the third paragraph can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissive of their characterization and confident that it rests on a simple misreading of the Alderney decisions

choices.label: B
choices.text: sympathetic to their concerns and persuaded that the traditional rule has been effectively abandoned

choices.label: C
choices.text: partially receptive but ultimately unconvinced, holding that the criticism captures a real difficulty yet overstates its consequences

choices.label: D
choices.text: uncertain whether the criticism is well founded and unwilling to reach a judgment on the question

choices.label: E
choices.text: openly hostile to the critics' methods while conceding the accuracy of their conclusions

explanations.correct: The author says the charge 'has some force' — the distinction between 'known' and 'foreseeable' peril is finer than the court has admitted — but then insists 'the criticism overstates the case.' That is exactly the 'partially receptive but ultimately unconvinced' posture.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author concedes the criticism has some force; he does not dismiss it as a misreading.
explanations.B: Mischaracterizes the author's conclusion, which is that the rule has been modified but not abandoned.
explanations.D: The author reaches a definite judgment; he is not simply undecided.
explanations.E: Out of register — there is nothing hostile in the author's treatment, and he does not concede the critics' conclusions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longstanding doctrine is described; a series of judicial modifications is traced; a critical view of those modifications is presented and partly rebutted; the author offers a concluding characterization.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two rival doctrines are introduced; evidence for each is surveyed; the author endorses the more recent and rejects the older.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine is described; its origins are traced to an early illustrative case; an opposing doctrine in a neighboring jurisdiction is compared; the two are shown to be equivalent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal rule is defended on policy grounds; objections to the policy defense are presented; the author concedes the objections and endorses a replacement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A series of cases is summarized in chronological order; a general principle is derived from the series; the principle is shown to resolve a longstanding doctrinal controversy.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 sets out the traditional rule and its rationale; paragraph 2 traces the Alderney court's known-peril exception and its extension; paragraph 3 states the critics' charge and partially rebuts it; paragraph 4 offers the concluding characterization of 'gradual domestication.'
explanations.B: The passage does not present two rival doctrines and endorse one; it describes modifications to a single doctrine.
explanations.C: The neighboring-jurisdiction comparison is a brief contrast in the final paragraph, not an equivalence demonstration.
explanations.D: The author does not concede the objections or endorse a replacement.
explanations.E: No general principle is derived from the cases; the passage traces qualifications to an existing rule.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the known-peril exception as developed by the Alderney High Court currently applies to which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: any trespasser whose presence a reasonable occupier would have foreseen

choices.label: B
choices.text: only children who wander onto unfenced land and cannot appreciate warning signs

choices.label: C
choices.text: adult trespassers whose presence the occupier has, as a factual matter, anticipated

choices.label: D
choices.text: trespassers injured by dangers that the occupier could have discovered through reasonable inspection

choices.label: E
choices.text: licensees and invitees who enter the land with the occupier's implied consent

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 reports that the exception was extended from children to 'adult trespassers whose presence was, as a factual matter, anticipated by the occupier.' That is the scope the doctrine has reached.
explanations.A: Altered qualifier: the author emphasizes that the court has refused to equate the 'known' peril standard with what a reasonable occupier would have foreseen.
explanations.B: Wrong sentence — the exception was originally limited to children, but the passage reports it has since been extended.
explanations.D: The third paragraph expressly states that the court has refused to require affirmative inspection for hidden dangers.
explanations.E: Outside scope — the passage does not address the occupier's duty to licensees or invitees.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine can be significantly modified by courts without being formally abandoned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The distinction between a known peril and a foreseeable one is of no practical consequence in landowner-liability cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The traditional rule concerning trespassers ought to be replaced with an undifferentiated negligence standard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts in neighboring jurisdictions have reached results more defensible than those of the Alderney High Court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The future of the known-peril exception is secure against further doctrinal pressure.

explanations.correct: The author's concluding image of 'gradual domestication' — the traditional rule qualified but not abandoned — commits him to the general proposition that significant modification need not amount to formal abandonment.
explanations.B: Reverses the author: he says the distinction collapses in practice, but denies that it is of no consequence — the court has used it to refuse extension to unanticipated trespassers.
explanations.C: The author is describing, not endorsing, that alternative approach, and his tone suggests a preference for the Alderney court's reticence.
explanations.D: Outside scope — the author contrasts the approaches without ranking them.
explanations.E: The closing 'regrettably, uncertain' implies the author is skeptical that the reticence will survive.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference in the second paragraph to commuters using an unmarked path across a rail yard functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the expansion of the known-peril exception beyond its original application to children

choices.label: B
choices.text: suggest that the Alderney High Court has applied the doctrine in ways that are difficult to defend on policy grounds

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast the Alderney doctrine with the approach of neighboring jurisdictions

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce a counterexample that the author believes the court should not have accepted

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why the traditional rule on trespassers has survived despite repeated judicial modification

explanations.correct: The commuter reference appears in the sentence that extends the exception 'to adult trespassers whose presence was, as a factual matter, anticipated' — paired with hikers as examples of that extension. Its rhetorical job is to illustrate the expansion.
explanations.B: Accurate-content, wrong-function: the author does not treat the commuter example as a policy failure.
explanations.C: The contrast with neighboring jurisdictions appears in the closing paragraph, not here.
explanations.D: The author reports the extension without suggesting the court erred in accepting it.
explanations.E: Wrong grain — the reference illustrates an expansion, not a survival.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the criticism discussed in the third paragraph overstates the case?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A recent empirical study of Alderney trial courts has found that judges applying the known-peril exception almost invariably find the occupier to have anticipated the trespasser's presence whenever a reasonable occupier would have foreseen it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several neighboring jurisdictions have expressly adopted the Alderney approach and applied it without reported difficulty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Landowners in Alderney report that they now take greater precautions against trespasser injuries than they did before the 1981 decision.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In cases involving child trespassers, Alderney courts continue to apply the known-peril exception more readily than in cases involving adults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Alderney legislature has considered, but declined to enact, a statute replacing the traditional trespasser rule with an undifferentiated negligence standard.

explanations.correct: The author's defense of the court rests on the claim that 'known' and 'foreseeable' peril are treated as distinct inquiries in practice. An empirical showing that trial courts collapse the two in application directly undercuts that defense and strengthens the critics' charge that the doctrine is functionally indistinguishable from ordinary negligence.
explanations.B: Wrong direction — adoption elsewhere says nothing about whether the distinction holds up in Alderney.
explanations.C: Greater landowner precaution is consistent with either side of the debate; it does not speak to the doctrinal distinction.
explanations.D: Off-target — this supports the author's picture of a differentiated doctrine, if anything.
explanations.E: Legislative inaction affects neither the court's application of the exception nor the critics' descriptive claim about its practical scope.

passage:
When constitutional courts are asked to interpret open-textured provisions — clauses guaranteeing "due process," "equal treatment," or "the liberty of the person" — two broad methodological camps tend to form. The first, often labeled originalist, insists that such provisions must be given the meaning they bore at the time of their enactment; to permit the language to shift with evolving social conditions, on this view, is to license judges to amend the constitution under cover of interpretation. The second, the living-document camp, treats the constitution as a text whose general terms are designed precisely to accommodate changing circumstances, and which must be read anew in each generation if it is to continue to govern a society its drafters could not have foreseen.

The debate, as it is usually staged, presents the two positions as exhaustive rivals. The Supreme Court of the fictitious Republic of Verrania, in a notable 2004 decision interpreting that country's 1867 guarantee of "liberty," offered what it called a third way. Writing for a narrow majority, Chief Justice Harmon argued that the historical meaning of a constitutional term fixes what she termed its outer limits — the scope beyond which no interpretation may go — while leaving room for the court to select, from among the readings that remain within those limits, the one best suited to contemporary conditions. A constitutional guarantee, on this view, is neither a photograph of the drafters' intentions nor a blank check to be filled in by each generation of judges.

The position has obvious appeal. It preserves the discipline of historical inquiry without committing the court to the anachronism of imagining itself in the drafters' shoes on every question. Yet the Harmon formulation is more difficult to apply than its economy of phrase suggests. The question of how the "outer limits" of a term's historical meaning are to be fixed is itself deeply contested, and the court's opinions have been less than forthcoming about the methodology. In some cases, those limits have been drawn with reference to ordinary eighteenth-century usage; in others, with reference to specialist legal dictionaries; in still others, with reference to the purposes the drafters are thought to have been pursuing. These sources do not always converge, and the Verranian court has not told us how to choose among them when they diverge.

For this reason, some commentators have charged that the Harmon formulation is not so much a middle position as a rhetorical concession to originalism, one that permits the court to reach living-document results while invoking the vocabulary of historical fidelity. That charge is probably unfair. The court has, in several decisions since 2004, refused to adopt interpretations that commentators on the living-document side had urged, precisely on the ground that the proposed readings exceeded the outer limits of the 1867 language. What is true is that the methodology remains undertheorized. Until the court addresses that deficiency, the promise of a third way will not be fully redeemed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Verranian Supreme Court's 2004 decision demonstrated that originalism and the living-document approach are not, as usually supposed, exhaustive alternatives for interpreting open-textured constitutional provisions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chief Justice Harmon's attempt to articulate a third way between originalism and the living-document approach is promising but remains methodologically incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commentators who charge that the Harmon formulation is merely a rhetorical concession to originalism have correctly identified the central weakness of the Verranian court's post-2004 jurisprudence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Constitutional courts ought to reject both originalism and the living-document approach in favor of a formulation that draws the outer limits of constitutional terms by reference to the purposes of the drafters.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Verranian court's 2004 decision interpreting the 1867 guarantee of liberty has been applied so inconsistently that it should be reconsidered by the full court.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the two-camp debate, presents Harmon's third way, notes its appeal, identifies the unspecified methodology for drawing outer limits as its central weakness, and closes by saying the promise will not be redeemed until that deficiency is addressed. B captures both the promise and the incompleteness.
explanations.A: Paragraph-level restatement of paragraph 2; the passage's overall argument goes beyond merely showing the two camps are not exhaustive.
explanations.C: The author expressly says this charge 'is probably unfair.'
explanations.D: The author does not endorse any particular source for outer limits; the purposes-of-the-drafters source is mentioned as one among several.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author does not call for reconsideration by the full court.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Chief Justice Harmon's formulation can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of its conceptual elegance and confidence in its practical application

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured approval of its theoretical aspiration tempered by concern about an unresolved methodological issue

choices.label: C
choices.text: pointed skepticism that treats the formulation as a rhetorical cover for results-driven decision making

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral curiosity about a novel approach whose merits he is unwilling to evaluate

choices.label: E
choices.text: disappointment with a promising beginning that the court has since abandoned in practice

explanations.correct: The author grants that the position has 'obvious appeal' and defends the court against the harsher critics, but insists the methodology for fixing outer limits is 'undertheorized' and that the promise will not be redeemed until that is addressed. That is measured approval plus a specific reservation.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity: the author raises a serious methodological concern.
explanations.C: The author expressly says the pointed-skeptic charge is 'probably unfair.'
explanations.D: The author does take a position, both in defending the court against commentators and in identifying a deficiency.
explanations.E: Wrong feature: the author does not say the court has abandoned the formulation; he says the court has applied it, if imperfectly.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the Harmon formulation treats the historical meaning of a constitutional term as

choices.label: A
choices.text: a source of guidance that judges may consult or disregard in light of contemporary conditions

choices.label: B
choices.text: the single correct reading from which no departure is permissible

choices.label: C
choices.text: a boundary that no interpretation may cross, within which the court selects the reading best suited to present conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: a photograph of the drafters' intentions that controls interpretation in every case

choices.label: E
choices.text: a starting point that is ordinarily dispositive but may be overridden when social circumstances have changed dramatically

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 reports that Harmon treats historical meaning as fixing the term's 'outer limits — the scope beyond which no interpretation may go — while leaving room for the court to select, from among the readings that remain within those limits, the one best suited to contemporary conditions.'
explanations.A: Altered qualifier: Harmon treats historical meaning as a binding outer limit, not as optional guidance.
explanations.B: Reverses the formulation: multiple readings remain permissible within the outer limits.
explanations.D: The passage uses the 'photograph of the drafters' intentions' language as something Harmon rejects.
explanations.E: Nothing in the formulation permits the outer limits themselves to be overridden.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court adopting the Harmon formulation should ordinarily give controlling weight to eighteenth-century ordinary usage over the drafters' apparent purposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The living-document approach is, on reflection, incompatible with any meaningful discipline of historical inquiry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The persuasiveness of the Harmon formulation would be increased if the court articulated how to adjudicate between conflicting sources of historical meaning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Originalism is preferable to the living-document approach because it provides a more determinate methodology.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commentators on the living-document side have been essentially correct in the specific interpretations they have urged since 2004.

explanations.correct: The author identifies the unresolved question of how to choose among divergent sources of historical meaning as the reason the formulation 'remains undertheorized,' and says the third way's promise will not be redeemed until that deficiency is addressed. He thus commits to the proposition that addressing that question would increase the formulation's persuasiveness.
explanations.A: The author describes ordinary usage as one source among several and does not rank it above the drafters' purposes.
explanations.B: Outside scope — the author does not claim the living-document approach cannot accommodate historical discipline.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse originalism; he describes a third way that seeks to combine historical discipline with interpretive latitude.
explanations.E: The passage reports that the court has rejected several living-document readings on historical grounds without indicating the author's view on the merits of those readings.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion in the third paragraph of the varying sources used to draw outer limits in different Verranian cases serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish that the Harmon formulation has been applied inconsistently across different subject-matter areas

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide support for the charge that the court has used the formulation as a rhetorical cover for results-driven decisions

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the particular methodological question the author believes the court has left unanswered

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that historical inquiry is more difficult in constitutional law than in other areas of law

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast the court's post-2004 practice with the methodology Chief Justice Harmon described in her 2004 opinion

explanations.correct: The paragraph catalogs ordinary usage, specialist dictionaries, and drafters' purposes precisely to pose the question the court has not answered: how to choose among them when they diverge. That is the unresolved methodological question the author flags.
explanations.A: Accurate-content, wrong-function: the author uses the variation to identify a gap in methodology, not to catalog subject-matter inconsistency.
explanations.B: The author expressly rejects the rhetorical-cover charge as 'probably unfair.'
explanations.D: Outside scope — the passage does not compare constitutional law with other areas.
explanations.E: The author does not claim the post-2004 practice departs from Harmon's stated methodology; he claims the stated methodology was never sufficiently specified.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's defense of the Harmon formulation against the charge made by the commentators in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In every post-2004 case in which the Verranian court has adopted a reading urged by living-document commentators, the reading was also consistent with ordinary eighteenth-century usage of the relevant term.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The commentators who have made the rhetorical-cover charge are themselves committed to the living-document approach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recent comparative study has found that courts in other jurisdictions invoking Harmon's formulation have disagreed about how to draw outer limits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chief Justice Harmon has retired, and the current Verranian court contains no justice who participated in the 2004 decision.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several constitutional scholars have praised the 2004 opinion as a significant contribution to interpretive theory.

explanations.correct: The author's defense turns on the court's having refused interpretations that exceeded the outer limits of historical meaning. If every living-document reading the court accepted was also within ordinary historical usage, then the court's post-2004 record coheres with the stated methodology rather than just reaching desired outcomes under historical vocabulary — directly strengthening the defense.
explanations.B: The commentators' own commitments do not bear on whether the charge is accurate.
explanations.C: Wrong direction — confusion about outer limits in other jurisdictions, if anything, weakens confidence in the formulation.
explanations.D: Personnel changes say nothing about whether the formulation was methodologically cover for results-driven decisions.
explanations.E: General scholarly praise is too diffuse to speak to the specific charge.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following hypothetical judicial rulings most closely conforms to the Harmon formulation as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "freedom of assembly" holds that the guarantee must be read to reflect contemporary social conditions, without reference to the meaning the term bore at enactment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "unreasonable search" determines that the eighteenth-century meaning of "unreasonable" forecloses any reading protective of electronic communications and declines on that basis to extend the guarantee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "cruel punishment" surveys the range of practices the eighteenth-century drafters would have regarded as cruel, concludes that prolonged solitary confinement falls within that range, and so holds the practice unconstitutional.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "due process" establishes that the term's historical meaning permits several readings, rejects a proposed reading as falling outside that permissible range, and adopts among the remaining readings the one best adapted to present circumstances.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court interpreting a constitutional guarantee of "equal protection" defers to the legislature's determination of what equal protection requires, citing the need to avoid judicial amendment of the constitution under cover of interpretation.

explanations.correct: The Harmon formulation has two operative features: (1) historical meaning fixes outer limits beyond which no reading may go, and (2) within those limits, the court selects the reading best suited to present conditions. D instantiates both features — rejection of an outside-the-limits reading, plus contemporary selection among the remaining readings.
explanations.A: Matches the living-document approach, which the Harmon formulation rejects as a blank check.
explanations.B: Applies only the outer-limits half of the formulation and stops there; it does not show the court selecting among permissible readings for present adaptation.
explanations.C: Does not exhibit the second operative feature: the court treats the eighteenth-century meaning as directly dispositive rather than as a limit within which a contemporary selection is made.
explanations.E: Describes judicial deference rather than the Harmon formulation, which concerns the court's own interpretive method.
